1.why: D accepts the meeting and adds a plausible spot; B is an ordinary counter-offer of a different time and nothing in the request rules it out. A asks a clarification the utterance never licenses; C is the only genuinely dead option.

2.why: C is the standard registrar/office answer. B (waiving on the student's word) is killed only by an institutional convention about written confirmation, not by anything the speaker said — a lenient clerk could utter it.

3.why: D accepts the proposed time and hedges on the stated choir conflict. C (Thursday mornings) is wrong only after inferring that 'choir has me Thursdays' blocks the day, which the utterance never states as all-day.

4.why: A saves the folder the speaker warned about. B is directly contradicted by 'has to be reimaged today'; C and D engage nothing the speaker asked.

5.why: A points out the ordering is impossible, but that impossibility exists only inside option A — the stimulus never says the upstairs keys open the tills. C is a plain, fully natural acceptance and nothing in the utterance defeats it.

6.why: A accepts the move. B is a normal reaction to hearing your Thursday slot is now free and nothing rules it out. Only D is properly killed (contradicted: the Thursday section no longer exists).

7.why: C is a counter-proposal on timing; B asks about lease length, which the utterance genuinely leaves open, so both are live. A and D are cleanly contradicted (the offer IS Elm; a single has no other bed).

8.why: D catches that the student was never told of a waiver. C answers the alternative question with 'neither' plus a reason and nothing in the utterance rules it out. A is only weakly odd (appealing a waived ticket), which is an inference, not a kill.

9.why: B is the natural 'I don't know, but she does' answer. D's clarification fails because nothing establishes more than one folding table — the utterance fails to license the question rather than ruling it out.

10.why: C resolves the tension the speaker themself flagged. D ('he's been unreliable all semester') is exactly what a friend would say to that complaint; it accepts a premise only an attentive listener would reject, which is an inference, not a rule-out.

11.why: C gives the status update sought. A's 'which one is it' is defeated only by inferring that two prior reports would have identified the machine. B is contradicted outright by 'reported twice', but B is not the runner-up.

12.why: A corrects the false premise: an emailed file never passed through a scanner. C (clean the glass, rerun) is wrong only once the listener draws that same inference; nothing in the words blocks it.

13.why: The responder is not identified as staff, so C ('mine's been doing that too, I'll flag it') is a fully natural peer reply. D (turn autosave on) is also live. Only A is arguably killed, and it kills itself by denying the speaker's report.

14.why: B fixes the mis-ring. A argues the merits of renting to someone who just said they are buying — it engages the wrong part of the utterance rather than being impossible.

15.why: The utterance never fixes whether the Friday paper falls before or after the Monday reopening. If after, D (accept the order) is right; if before, C is. The intended kill is pure under-determination, so both survive.

16.why: C answers the permission request by naming who actually holds it. B offers to rewrite the methods instead — it addresses the underlying goal, not the request, so it is off-target rather than false.

17.why: A accepts the Sunday routing; C ('does it still reach Hale before six?') is an equally natural follow-up and nothing in the utterance answers or forbids it. D is the one clean kill — 'no stops between' contradicts a drop-off.

18.why: The stimulus is informational, so C (act on it) and A (apologise, empty the box) and even B (agree) are all natural. Only D is killed, and killed well: it asks what was just stated.

19.why: B explains this reader and routes around it. C is contradicted — 'these readers all act up' cannot stand beside 'the others take it'. A and D blame the card, which the same clause refutes.

20.why: A yes/no offer with both a plain acceptance (B) and a sensible counter (A) present, and nothing in the utterance favouring either. D is the only real kill: the speaker already named the deadline.

21.why: The tutor offered, so accepting (A) is not ruled out by anything said; D declines and asks for flags instead. Whatever separates them is a tutoring norm the item never states.

22.why: 'How soon' calls for a time and only B gives one. A (some pages are in pencil) is a real thing to say but answers a different question; C is largely settled by 'if I keep your paper log'.

23.why: The asker's own words concede the specialist needs the slip back, so B follows and A is flatly contradicted. Runner-up C denies the requirement, which only fails once you infer the asker learned it from this office.

24.why: D accepts and names the blocker the speaker mentioned. B redirects to Marco, which neither answers 'tonight' nor solves the clipboard problem — off-target rather than impossible.

25.why: A accepts that it is in hand. B ('nobody's touched it since the weekend') is defeated only by inferring that maintenance being up there now makes the complaint stale. D is the clean contradiction but is the weakest option, not the runner-up.

26.why: A bare borrow request: lending (A) and declining (D) are both fully natural and the utterance settles nothing. Any preference for D comes from a meal-card policy the item never mentions.

27.why: D asks for the right advisor; A accepts cross-field practice, which many students would, and nothing rules it out. B is well killed — the speaker already said 'since you're pre-law', so there is nothing to correct.

28.why: The request is self-undermining as written (be there while you are away), so both C (restating that the clinical is all day) and A (someone must stay the whole time) are natural objections. The stimulus itself may be an authoring slip.

29.why: Only A answers 'how do I get Thursday'. D explains why the line is dead — true, responsive in tone, but it never supplies a route, so it is off-target. B is contradicted by the three unanswered voicemails.

30.why: D declines to sign for someone else. A is stopped only by the convention that you cannot sign another person's consent form — the words permit it, so the kill is normative, not logical.

31.why: The speaker uses 'the day we close early' as shared knowledge, so a listener who knows it can answer with A; a listener who does not asks D. The utterance does not settle which listener this is.

32.why: C answers the offer and keys off 'we've got left'. B praises the recycled stock without accepting or refusing — it engages the paper, not the offer.
